title: [Chapitre] II. Réalisations topologiques des réseaux : notes manuscrites (06/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 5-7). Grothendieck is building an intrinsic topological theory of 'ficelles' (strings). A ficelle is a pair F = (X, {A, B}), where X is a connected space and A, B are closed 'ends' that may be larger than points. It must satisfy axioms a)-d): no isolated ends, the relevant complements connected, and d) a local irreducibility / local connectedness condition. A 'lien' (link) of F is a closed subset C that cuts X into a part U_{A,C} on the A side and a part U_{B,C} on the B side. The aim, stated on p. 7, is to 'decouper' a ficelle along an interior link C into two ficelles F_{A,C} = (X_{A,C}, {A, C}) and F_{B,C}, with X equal to the union of X_{A,C} and X_{C,B} glued along C. The purpose is to realise the edges of a 'réseau' (graph or network) topologically, and later to form categories of ficelles with interior links and of pairs of ficelles glued at an end.

State before this page. On p. 5 he reduced to the case where the ends are points a, b, c. He checked that X_{A,C} = closure(U_{A,C}) ∪ C satisfies axioms a), b) and c). Only axiom d) remains open.

This page, step 1: Lemma. Let Z be a space and Z', Z'' closed subsets (implicitly with Z = Z' ∪ Z'') such that Z' ∩ Z'' = {c}. Then c has a connected neighbourhood in Z if and only if it has one in Z' and one in Z''.
- 'If': take connected neighbourhoods V' and V''. Their union is connected because both contain c. It is a neighbourhood in Z: if W' and W'' are open in Z with W' ∩ Z' ⊂ V' and W'' ∩ Z'' ⊂ V'', then W' ∩ W'' ⊂ V' ∪ V''.
- 'Only if': let V be a connected neighbourhood in Z. Then V ∩ Z' is connected. Indeed, suppose it splits as P ⊔ Q with c in P. Then Q misses Z''. So Q is open in V (it equals O ∩ (V \ Z'')) and closed in V, which contradicts the connectedness of V.

Step 2: consequence. With Z = X, Z' = X_{A,C} and Z'' = X_{C,B}, the lemma transfers axiom d) at c between X and the two pieces. So the only thing left for the decomposition into links is to state the extra condition: C is not one of the ends (C ∉ {A, B}) and X is locally connected along C, or C is suitably locally connected in U = X \ (A ∪ B).

Step 3: example. For small t, the 'spheres' (frontiers) of U_{A,t}, written U̇_{A,t} = S_{A,t}, are links of the ficelle. The sets U_{A,t} are presumably metric or tubular neighbourhoods of the end A, defined on an earlier page.

Step 4: disjoint links. On the set L(F) of links he defines a symmetric relation 'C and D are disjoint':
- disjointness always implies C ≠ D;
- if C or D lies in {A, B}, it simply means distinct;
- otherwise it means C ∩ D = ∅.
The diagonal margin works out the case analysis (for instance, if D ∈ {A, B} then ... {C, D} = {A, B}) and a characterisation of when C is a link: C ⊂ U, and so on. This prepares the 'betweenness' lemma of p. 7: D is a link of F_{B,C} if and only if C is a link of F_{A,D}. That lemma gives a linear order on links, as in the cut-point order of an arc.
errors: The lemma as written omits the hypothesis Z = Z' ∪ Z''. It is needed for 'if', since otherwise V' ∪ V'' need not be a neighbourhood in Z. Context makes the hypothesis clear.

The lemma speaks of 'a connected neighbourhood', whereas axiom d) presumably needs local connectedness, i.e. a fundamental system of connected neighbourhoods. The same proof works for bases, so this is only a phrasing gap.
The precise extra condition ('C ... localement connexe dans U') is left only sketched; the page does not finish it.

ideas.what: Local connectedness at a wedge point: c is locally connected in Z' ∪ Z'' (two closed pieces meeting in c) if and only if it is so in each piece.
ideas.modern_name: Local connectedness of a one-point union (wedge) of closed subspaces

ideas.what: Axiomatic 'ficelles' (strings with closed sets as ends) and their 'liens' (separating closed sets), as building blocks for topological realisations of networks.
ideas.modern_name: Arcs, or more generally continua irreducible between two closed sets; cut sets / separators (Moore-Kline characterisation of the arc via non-cut points)
ideas.usually_credited_to: R. L. Moore (1920), J. R. Kline, Whyburn (analytic topology)

ideas.what: Small spheres S_{A,t} around an end are links of the ficelle.
ideas.modern_name: Level sets of a distance or tubular function as separators

ideas.what: A 'disjointness' relation on the set of links, preparing a betweenness / linear order on links.
ideas.modern_name: Separation order of cut sets in an irreducible continuum

missed.claim: Grothendieck's 1986 programme to define topological realisations of 'réseaux' through an intrinsic axiomatic theory of ficelles and their links, cut and glued along links, was never developed or published. It overlaps substantially with classical continuum theory, which he does not cite.
missed.quote: Il y a donc seulement, pour avoir décomposition de la ficelle en liens, d'exprimer la condition
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly of historical interest: it documents a late attempt at a 'tame' foundation for graph realisations, related to the Esquisse themes. The mathematics on this page is classical point-set topology.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine point-set topology (a wedge lemma and a disjointness relation) inside an unpublished, mostly classical reconstruction of arc and continuum theory. Historically mildly interesting, but there is no new result.
transcription_corrections: 'C ⊄ {A,B}' should most likely read 'C ∉ {A,B}': C is an element (a link), not a subset of the set of ends.
'd'exprimer la condition' (fine); 'en liens [?]' is plausibly 'en liens' (links); the next page's transcription 'lieu' is probably also 'lien'.
The lemma's final clause reads 'qu'il ait un voisinage connexe dans Z' et Z''', with 'connexe dans' inserted above the line.
The word 'Exemple' appears struck through and reworked, with the insertion '(cf. ... P)' and a '(+)' referring to the marginal note.
